title: How to Use Real Estate to Supplement Retirement Income
description: Generating 'Mailbox Money' to cover fixed expenses in retirement.
content:
A stock portfolio requires you to sell shares to generate cash, which is terrifying during a crash. Real estate generates cash (rent) without selling the asset. This 'Cash Flow' feature makes real estate a favorite tool for retirees. By building a portfolio of rentals or REITs, you can create a 'salary' that covers your basic bills, leaving your stock portfolio to grow for luxuries or inflation protection. This guide explores how to integrate property into a withdrawal strategy.

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Cover the Basics' Strategy: Aim to have enough net rental income to cover your property taxes, utilities, and food. If your 'Survival Costs' are covered by rent, stock market volatility doesn't matter.
  • De-Leveraging: Entering retirement with mortgaged rentals is risky. One vacancy can cause a cash crunch. The goal should be to pay off rental mortgages before retiring to maximize cash flow.
  • REITs for Passive Income: If you don't want to unplug toilets at 70, swap physical rentals for REIT ETFs (VNQ). They pay ~4% dividends and require zero work.
  • 1031 Exchange to Passive: Use a 1031 exchange to sell high-maintenance apartments and buy low-maintenance 'Triple Net' commercial properties or DSTs (Delaware Statutory Trusts).

Why It Matters (US Context)

Depreciation recapture and capital gains taxes are huge when selling rentals. 'Die with the property' is often the best tax strategy (Step-Up in Basis for heirs). If you need to sell, do it strategically.

Real Estate vs. The 4% Rule

Comparing a $500,000 Stock Portfolio vs. a $500,000 Rental Property (Paid Off).

Option A: Stocks ($500k)

4% Rule: Safe withdrawal of $20,000/year.
Pros: Liquid, no work.
Cons: Income fluctuates. Principal can drop.

Option B: Rental House ($500k)

Gross Rent: $3,500/mo ($42k/yr).
Expenses (Tax/Ins/Maint): $1,500/mo ($18k/yr).
Net Income: $24,000/year.
Pros: Higher income (4.8% yield). Rents rise with inflation.
Cons: Illiquid. Work required. Concentration risk.

Verdict: Real Estate creates a higher 'Safe Withdrawal Rate', but requires labor.

The Transition Plan

  1. The 'Snowball' Payoff: 10 years before retirement, stop buying new properties. Use the cash flow from all units to pay off one mortgage at a time. Enter retirement with 3 paid-off houses rather than 10 leveraged ones.
  2. Hire Management: Budget 10% of rent for a Property Manager. You do not want to be a landlord at 75. If the deal doesn't pencil with a manager, sell it.
  3. DST (Delaware Statutory Trust): A way to 1031 exchange into a massive commercial property owned by hundreds of investors. Totally passive. Good for estate planning.
  4. Reverse Mortgage Option: Use a HECM on your primary home to delay selling investment properties during a downturn.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I sell my rentals to retire?

It triggers a massive tax bill (Recapture + Capital Gains). It is usually better to keep them for income or 1031 exchange them. Only sell if you need the lump sum liquidity.

Are REITs taxed higher?

Yes. REIT dividends are 'ordinary income' (mostly), not qualified dividends. Hold VNQ in your IRA to avoid the tax drag.

What if tenants stop paying?

This is 'Vacancy Risk'. You need a 6-month cash reserve for each property. Do not retire without this buffer.
